label: map_1
name: One-way pykrete flood barges
mech: In winter, shallow moulds on the frozen banks of a river near the mine are flooded with river water mixed with sawdust, and the cold freezes them into thick pykrete hulls. Ore concentrate is sealed inside these hulls in waterproof bags. At spring breakup the hulls float free and ride the flood hundreds of kilometres downstream to an Arctic port or rail point. There the cargo is lifted out and the hull is simply left to melt. A short GPS and ice-thickness log for each hull is used to adjust next year's hull thickness and launch dates to the river's real flood behaviour.
value: Bulk cargo can leave roadless deposits once a year with no steel fleet, no return trips and no road, using a free current and a hull that costs almost nothing.

label: map_1
name: Frost-wedge in-situ ore shattering
mech: In autumn, a dense grid of cheap boreholes is drilled into the ore body and flooded with water. Winter air is then blown or naturally drawn through them, so the water freezes and expands by about 9%. Repeated over several freeze-thaw cycles, this splits the rock along its grain boundaries into fine fragments. Temperature and acoustic sensors in the boreholes record where cracking has slowed, and the next year's water injection is concentrated in those zones. In the thaw season the fines are washed or vacuumed out instead of being blasted and crushed.
value: Most of the cost of blasting, explosives transport and crushing disappears, because the Arctic climate breaks the rock for free.

label: map_1
name: Winter freeze-concentration of leachates
mech: A dilute leach solution or brine carrying metals or rare earths is sprayed or spread in thin layers over a sloped field during winter. Freezing pushes the dissolved salts out of the pure ice, and the concentrated liquid drains away into collecting channels. The spraying rate and the number of passes are adjusted from conductivity readings at the outlet until the target concentration is reached. The ice left behind is nearly clean water that is reused in spring.
value: Concentrating metals before shipping, normally an energy-hungry step, becomes nearly free, so only a small volume of high-grade liquor has to leave the site.

label: map_3
name: Grown pykrete drift barges
mech: In winter, crews repeatedly flood thin layers of river water mixed with wood-chip waste onto riverbank ice. This builds pykrete slabs about 100x30x5 m, each able to float roughly 1,000 t of bagged ore concentrate. The cargo is loaded on top while everything is frozen. At spring breakup the slab floats free, and small tugs steer it down the Lena or Yenisei to an Arctic transshipment port. There it is unloaded and left to melt, so no barge has to go back upstream.
value: Each spring flood becomes a one-way bulk fleet whose only materials are water, sawdust and frost.

label: map_3
name: Cable-hauled ice guideway sleds
mech: Sprinkler rigs build a narrow, graded ice trough along a fixed line from a deposit to a railhead or river. They refresh it automatically whenever the temperature drops enough. Steel-runner ore sleds clip onto an endless steel cable loop, like a ski lift, driven by motors at the two ends. Because runners on ice have friction close to rail, a single loop moves a continuous stream of cargo without trucks, drivers or road surface. Sensors on the track trigger re-spraying wherever the ice wears down.
value: Gives near-railway freight costs every winter for the price of a cable, two winches and a water pump.

label: map_3
name: Permafrost-sealed in-place leaching
mech: Blasting breaks up the ore body underground, and circulating warm brine thaws only a bounded block of it. A leaching solution is then pumped through the block to dissolve the metal, and wells recover it. Any liquid that leaks toward the edge of the block refreezes on contact with the surrounding frozen ground, so the permafrost acts as a self-healing container. Temperature readings at the boundary show where the seal is. Only the recovered metal, often under 1% of the ore's mass, is ever transported.
value: Extracts metals from remote frozen deposits with no pit, no ore haulage and no artificial liner.

label: map_2
name: Disposable Pykrete Flood Barges
mech: In winter, crews cast barge hulls on the frozen river surface near the mine. The hulls are made of pykrete: water frozen with 10-15% local larch sawdust or pulp, which is several times tougher than plain ice. They are filled with ore concentrate or coal and capped with a sprayed ice-and-sawdust lid, insulated with a layer of sawdust. When the ice breaks up in spring, the flood floats them north to an estuary. GPS beacons report their drift, and a few tugs gather them for transfer to sea ships. The hulls are never brought back: they melt into the river, so the transport fleet costs almost nothing to build and needs no return trip. The hull wall thickness and the cargo load are set each year from flood forecasts and from strength tests of the frozen hulls.
value: Any deposit near a north-flowing river can ship bulk cargo once a year with no road, railway or permanent fleet.

label: map_2
name: Autonomous Kite-Sled Freight Trains
mech: Driverless trains of sleds cross frozen tundra and coastal sea ice pulled by large controllable traction kites, like those used to tow ships and on polar expeditions, scaled to tonnes per sled. A small onboard computer steers the kite, picks a route from wind forecasts and ice thickness maps, and anchors the train to wait out calm or unfavourable wind. Each train stores its route log and the ice conditions it meets, and the shared route map improves every season. It has no fuel, road or driver costs, and slow delivery is acceptable for ore stockpiled over the winter.
value: It replaces diesel winter-road trucking with nearly free wind power over the roadless distances where trucking costs the most.

label: map_2
name: Engineered Frost-Shatter Comminution
mech: Broken ore is stacked in insulated heaps laced with pipes and saturated with water. Fans then alternate −40°C winter air with warm water heated by waste heat from stranded gas or a generator. This runs many freeze-thaw cycles per winter instead of one per year. Water expands about 9% when it freezes, which forces cracks open along grain boundaries and shatters the rock to fine sizes. Temperature and acoustic sensors in the heap detect when cracking stops, and the cycle timing is adjusted to match.
value: Most of the crushing and grinding energy, the largest energy cost in hard-rock mining, is replaced by free Arctic cold, so remote deposits can be heap-leached or concentrated on site.

label: g1_genius
name: Transpolar Drift Freight
mech: Sealed, buoyant ore containers with satellite tags are set into Laptev Sea fast ice near the Lena delta. The Transpolar Drift carries the ice and containers to Fram Strait in 2–3 years without fuel or escort. When the floes melt, the containers float in open water and ships pick them up by their tag positions.
value: Bulk ore can reach European waters with no icebreakers, paying only the cost of time.

label: g1_genius
name: Winter-Only Railway
mech: Track panels are laid straight onto snow-compacted frozen tundra, with no permanent embankment, and rivers are crossed on artificially thickened ice. The line runs only during the 5–6 months when the ground is rigid. Each autumn, tamping machines re-level the track to undo the summer heave.
value: Rail-scale bulk capacity reaches remote deposits for a fraction of the cost of an all-season Arctic railway.

label: g1_genius
name: Frozen Placer Dry-Washing
mech: In deep winter, frozen placer gravel is dug and crushed while it stays below −20 °C. At that temperature the ice behaves as a brittle, light mineral. Air tables and dry-washers separate the gold and heavy minerals from gravel and ice by density, with no water at all, and the tailings are stacked frozen.
value: Placer mining can run all year without thawing, water or tailings ponds.

label: g1_mech
name: Buoyant Under-Ice Current Packets
mech: Sealed sacks of about 1 t of ground valuable material each carry a gas bladder, set so the sack is slightly lighter than water and rides pressed against the smooth underside of a frozen river. The current under the ice, which flows all winter, pushes them 25–50 km a day with no fuel or vessel. If a pressure sensor detects a stall, a valve lets out gas so the sack drops back into the flow, then refills it from a cartridge. A net under a slot cut in the ice collects the sacks far downstream.
value: Freight moves along frozen rivers through the whole winter at almost no energy cost, when today nothing moves on them.

label: g1_mech
name: Cold-Dry-Air Charge Sorting
mech: Crushed dry rock is tumbled against a plate so that different minerals pick up different electric charges. The near-zero moisture of −40 °C air stops that charge from leaking away. The grains fall between two charged plates and are pushed into separate bins according to their charge. Readings from each bin continuously adjust the plate voltage and the dividers between bins.
value: Valuable material is separated from waste on site through the winter with no water, cutting the tonnage to be hauled by 5–20 times.

label: g1_mech
name: Stored Meltwater Barge Pulse
mech: In winter, sprayed water builds an ice wall across a small creek, and a peat cover keeps it from melting. Snowmelt fills the basin behind it, and the water is released through a gate in midsummer as a timed crest. Flat-bottomed barges ride the crest down to a river deep enough for ships. Downstream depth gauges control the gate opening so the crest stays deeper than the barges' draft for the whole distance.
value: Creeks that are too shallow for boats become seasonal freight routes from remote deposits, with no road or dredging.

label: g1_core
name: Relay flood-pulse ore barges
mech: Inflatable rubber weirs are flown in folded and set up in series on a small tributary between the deposit and a navigable river; each pond fills with snowmelt and rain. Shallow-draft barges loaded with concentrate wait in the top pond. A hydraulic routing model times the gate releases so that each pulse lifts the barges over the next shallow stretch into the pond below, and the model re-plans from water-level gauges after every pulse. Empty barges are winched back across the flat pools, and the weirs are deflated after the season, leaving no road or rail.
value: Turns an ordinary summer stream into a temporary waterway, so bulk tonnage moves at water-freight cost without building a corridor.

label: g1_core
name: Seasonal thermal-diode ground thaw
mech: Each spring, black UV-stable geotextile is laid over the deposit to absorb round-the-clock summer sun. Each autumn, rows of cheap snow fences are set up to trap a thick snow blanket that blocks most winter refreezing. Buried temperature strings track the thaw front, and film coverage and fence spacing are re-tuned every season to maximise net heat gain, so the unfrozen zone deepens year after year. Light rippers and loaders can then dig the thawed gravel without blasting or heavy frozen-ground machinery.
value: Replaces diesel-intensive excavation of frozen ground with free solar heat for placers and shallow overburden.

label: g1_core
name: Midnight-sun salt-gradient power pond
mech: An insulated, lined pond holds a salinity gradient made from local Siberian Platform brines. The gradient traps summer insolation in the dense bottom layer at 60–80 °C, and in winter the ice lid adds insulation. In winter an organic Rankine cycle draws heat from the bottom layer and rejects it to −40 °C air. That temperature difference of about 110 K roughly doubles the efficiency of solar-pond plants in temperate climates. Gradient sensors trigger brine injection whenever the non-convecting layer starts to mix.
value: Supplies winter heat and electricity to remote operations from local salt and sunlight, cutting the fuel that has to come in by winter road.

label: g1_core2
name: Etched thermokarst freight canals
mech: The surface of ice-rich yedoma is stripped or darkened along a planned line toward a navigable river, while insulating mats protect the banks as a mask. Each summer, meltwater ponds in the strip, absorbs more sun and deepens the thaw. Mud drains away until thawing stops at ice-poor ground, leaving a channel deep enough for barges. Ground-temperature probes guide each year's re-darkening and widening, like etch-rate control.
value: Solar heat does the digging, so lowland deposits get a waterway for the cost of surface treatment instead of a road at millions of dollars per kilometre.

label: g1_core2
name: Fire-controlled ballistic ore transfer
mech: A gas or electric gun on the deposit fires steel-cased slugs of 100-500 kg of concentrate at about 1.5 km/s into a sand-and-water catch basin at a railhead or river port more than 100 km away. Radar measures where each round lands, and that miss distance corrects elevation and charge for the next round, exactly like artillery adjusting fire. Casings are recovered and sent back on the seasonal supply route.
value: A stranded deposit is connected to market by two fixed installations and no corridor at all.

label: g1_core2
name: Sub-ambient photonic permafrost shields
mech: Pads, embankments, tailings and foundations are covered with polymer radiative-cooling film. It reflects sunlight and radiates heat through the 8-13 µm atmospheric window, so the surface stays below air temperature even in the 24-hour summer sun. Buried thermistors show where the ground is warming, and more film layers or wider coverage go there.
value: Ice-rich ground stays frozen with no power, piles or thermosyphons, so foundations cost far less and stop failing.

label: g1_loop
name: Paid ore ballast on LNG carriers
mech: Ice-class LNG carriers leave Arctic terminals with full tanks but under their weight limit, so they also carry thousands of tonnes of seawater ballast. Sealed cassettes of briquetted concentrate, brought by barge from deposits on the Yenisei and Ob, take the place of that ballast in double-bottom spaces and are swapped for seawater at the port where the LNG is unloaded. For each voyage, cargo reports and the ship's draft from AIS tracking give the ratio of paid tonnes to available deadweight. That ratio sets how many cassettes the next loading plan assigns, turning ballast space into cargo space.
value: Arctic concentrate rides ships that already sail to Asian and European markets, at almost no extra cost for fuel or icebreakers.

label: g1_loop
name: Transpolar drift cargo pods
mech: Reusable sealed pods, shaped like Nansen's Fram so that ice pressure squeezes them upward instead of crushing them, are filled with coal or concentrate whose value does not suffer from slow delivery. In autumn they are set on newly formed Laptev Sea ice, drift with the ice to the ice edge at Fram Strait, and are picked up there by an ordinary ship. Comparing daily satellite radar maps of the ice gives drift paths traced backward from the Fram Strait exit. Starting sites whose paths turn off into the Beaufort Gyre are dropped, new sites are added where paths converge on the exit, and pod placement is re-optimized each season from beacon logs.
value: Bulk cargo moves from the Laptev coast to the North Atlantic with no engines, no icebreakers and no infrastructure, trading about two years in transit for almost no freight cost.

label: g1_loop
name: Under-ice river drift pods
mech: In winter, slightly buoyant torpedo-shaped pods of concentrate are pushed through a slot cut in the ice of a big Siberian river's main channel. They ride the current along the smooth underside of the ice, out of reach of wind and waves, to a downstream recovery station with a boom and slot at a port. Weekly current profiles taken through the ice show where the flow stays fast. Where it slows, or where slush ice builds a dam below the ice, a relay slot is cut, the pods are lifted past the blockage and released again, and the spacing between releases is adjusted to the measured speed.
value: Ore reaches Arctic ports during the frozen months and is already on the quay, instead of competing for the short summer window on the river.

label: g2_evo2
name: Thaw-Front Self-Panning Placers
mech: The overburden is stripped from an ice-rich placer, and a shallow pond of meltwater is kept on top so it absorbs round-the-clock summer sun. Each summer the top layer thaws, and its excess ground ice turns it into a weak, saturated slurry. Gold and other heavy minerals sink through the slurry and settle on the still-frozen floor. Year by year the advancing thaw front carries this heavy layer down to bedrock. Ground-temperature probes track how deep the front has gone, and the pond depth is adjusted to speed it up or slow it down. Then only the thin enriched bottom layer is dug and washed.
value: Sunlight and gravity do most of the excavation and concentration, so a placer is mined by moving a few percent of the gravel that conventional digging moves.

label: g2_evo2
name: Drag-Diving Under-Ice Ore Spheres
mech: In winter, concentrate is packed into rigid spheres about 1 m across with closed-cell foam shells, which have no gas, valves or electronics. They are pushed through one slot cut in the ice of a large Siberian river's main channel. Each sphere's buoyancy is trimmed to roughly 0.5% above that of the water, so the drag of the current is larger than its lift. The sphere rolls along the smooth underside of the ice, and when it meets a hanging slush dam or an ice ridge, the current pushes it down and around. A boom under a slot at a downstream port collects the spheres, which are sent back upriver empty in summer.
value: Ore moves hundreds of kilometres to the quay all winter with no fuel, vehicle or tending, at a time when nothing else moves on these rivers.

label: g2_evo1
name: Snow-Masked Under-Ice Guide Groove
mech: In early winter, two parallel strips are cleared of snow along the fast main channel of a frozen river, while the snow between and beside them is left as insulation. Ice grows faster under the cleared strips, forming two downward keels with a smooth groove between them on the underside of the ice. Passive, slightly buoyant concentrate pods put in through a slot ride the groove on the current without drifting into slow water near the banks. Ice-thickness readings taken through the ice guide where the strips are cleared again after each snowfall.
value: It turns any large frozen river into a self-built winter conveyor for ore with no fuel, vessels or moving parts.

label: g2_evo1
name: Current-Washed Under-Ice Sluice
mech: A long riffled sluice box is hung beneath a slot cut in the ice of a river that keeps flowing all winter. Frozen placer gravel from a nearby deposit is crushed and dropped into the slot. The river's own 0 °C current, kept liquid by the ice lid, washes the gravel. Gold and heavy minerals settle in the riffles, and fine tailings disperse in the low winter flow. The sluice is lifted weekly through the slot to collect the concentrate, and its angle is set from flow speeds measured through the ice.
value: Placer gold can be washed through the whole winter with no pumps, heated plant or tailings ponds.

label: g2_evo1
name: Wind-Sublimation Ore Drying
mech: Frozen, ice-rich ore or wet concentrate is spread in thin layers on pads exposed to the dry, windy −30 °C air of deep winter. Ice turns straight into vapour without melting, at roughly 1 kg/m² a day, and a harrow turns the layers. Moisture probes decide when each strip is dry enough to be swept up and the next layer laid down.
value: It removes 20–50% of the hauled weight and gives dry material ready for dry separation, with no fuel or thermal dryers.

label: g2_imm
name: Metal Vapour Gas-Line Hitchhike
mech: At a nickel, cobalt or iron deposit close to a gas trunk line, a little of the line's gas is partly burned to make carbon monoxide. That carbon monoxide is passed over crushed, reduced ore at about 50 °C and a few bar, and the metal leaves as a volatile vapour (one nickel atom bound to four carbon monoxide molecules). The vapour is metered into the pipeline gas at about 0.1 mol%. That keeps it below its condensation pressure at line temperatures, and dosing follows measured flow and temperature. At the receiving plant, before any customer, the gas passes over beds heated to about 200 °C. The vapour splits there into pure metal pellets and carbon monoxide, which is burned or sent back.
value: A line carrying about 38 billion m³ a year could carry roughly 100,000 t of refined nickel a year at almost no extra transport cost, using infrastructure that is already built.

label: g2_imm
name: Oil-Line Dissolved-Metal Slugs
mech: At the deposit, an acid solution of gold, platinum-group metals, cobalt or rare earths is stirred with diesel-range oil that contains a metal-grabbing reagent, so the metal moves into the oil. The loaded oil goes into the crude trunk line as separate slugs between crude batches, about 2% of throughput, and density meters track each slug. At the coastal terminal each slug is cut into its own tank and washed with strong acid. The acid takes the metal back for plating out, and the cleaned oil is sold as ordinary fuel, so the carrier never has to come back.
value: Remote high-value metals reach a seaport for almost nothing by riding inside an existing oil pipeline. At 1 g/L that is up to about 2,000 t of metal a year.

label: g2_imm
name: Freezing-Water Winter Power Engine
mech: Water at 0–4 °C is pumped from under lake or river ice and sprayed over coils where propane or CO₂ boils. The water's warmth and the heat it gives off as it freezes boil the fluid, which drives a turbine. The fluid then condenses in finned radiators open to −35 to −50 °C air. About 30 kg/s of water turned to slush gives roughly 1 MW. The slush is piled into ice heaps, and output rises on its own as the air gets colder.
value: Remote deposits get fuel-free power for the seven-month winter, when crushing and haulage peak, and diesel no longer has to be trucked in.

label: ctrl_4
name: Melt-away pykrete flood barges
mech: Each winter, crews build barge hulls from pykrete (ice reinforced with sawdust, much stronger and tougher than plain ice) right on a frozen tributary near the deposit. They need only spray nozzles, local sawdust and -40°C air, and they load ore concentrate into the hulls on the spot. A forecast built from snowpack and river-gauge data sets the loading schedule for the spring breakup flood, which briefly makes thousands of otherwise unnavigable creeks deep enough to float the barges. A small pusher tows them to a railhead or Arctic river port, where they are emptied and left to melt. A hull costs little more than water, sawdust and labour, so the cost per tonne is a few weeks of towing rather than a road kept open all year.
value: Turns the spring flood on every remote tributary into near-free, single-use bulk freight capacity with no road, dredging or shipyard.

label: ctrl_4
name: Winter-cold brine fractionation ponds
mech: In winter, metal leach liquors or the Siberian Platform's lithium-bearing calcium-chloride brines are pumped into shallow lined ponds. Air at -40 to -55°C freezes pure ice out of them, and skimming it off concentrates the liquid without burning fuel for evaporation. As the pond cools past successive eutectic points, salts such as mirabilite, hydrohalite and magnesium chloride hydrates crystallise one after another and are harvested, leaving a liquor ever richer in the target metal. Temperature and density sensors time each harvest and decide when to move liquor to a colder pond. The skimmed ice is stockpiled as clean process water for summer.
value: Produces a refined, high-value product at a remote site using free cold, so only a small fraction of the original tonnage has to be transported.

label: ctrl_4
name: Transpolar drift cargo pods
mech: In winter, sealed and buoyant pods built to withstand ice pressure are filled with dense concentrate that does not spoil (nickel matte, rare-earth or tin concentrate) and placed on fast ice off the Lena delta. The Transpolar Drift, the current that carried Nansen's Fram, then moves them across the Arctic Basin to Fram Strait in roughly one to three years. Each pod carries a satellite beacon, and a drift model kept updated with beacon tracks and ice forecasts predicts where pods will exit. One ice-class vessel can then collect each season's arrivals in the East Greenland Current. Because the pods float if their floe breaks up, losses are limited to beacon failures and pods crushed in pressure ridges.
value: Moves concentrate from the Siberian shelf to Atlantic markets with no fuel and no icebreaker escort, trading speed for a slow but predictable supply pipeline.

label: ctrl_5
name: Frost-wedge rock fragmentation
mech: Instead of blasting, drill a grid of holes into the frozen orebody, fill them with water and seal each hole's top with a packer. The surrounding permafrost is below 0 °C, so each water column freezes from the wall inward. This traps the liquid core and pressurises it to tens of MPa, well above rock tensile strength (5–15 MPa): the burst-pipe effect at bench scale. Acoustic sensors log cracking in each hole, and software refills holes that cracked too little and adjusts hole spacing for the next bench.
value: Removes explosives from remote mines, along with the airlift, magazines and permits they need, cutting rock-breaking cost several-fold and allowing vibration-free mining next to settlements and infrastructure.

label: ctrl_5
name: Single-use pykrete river barges
mech: Each winter, pumps on a floodplain next to the mine's river spray water mixed with sawdust from local sawmills into moulds. It freezes layer by layer into pykrete hulls (ice with about 14% wood fibre, several times stronger than plain ice and much slower to melt), each carrying a few thousand tonnes. Concentrate or coal stockpiled over winter is loaded straight in, and the spring flood lifts the hulls off the floodplain and carries them north at 100–200 km/day, with one small pusher boat steering each convoy. At the delta port the cargo is moved to ships and the hull is left to melt; wall thickness is set each year from the forecast water temperature and the route length.
value: Winter cold and the spring flood become a free, throwaway fleet that moves bulk cargo from roadless interiors to Arctic ports with no steel hulls to build and no return trip.

label: ctrl_5
name: Transpolar Drift cargo pods
mech: At a port on the Laptev or East Siberian Sea, bulk cargo is loaded into rounded steel pods with no engines. Their shape makes ice pressure push them upward instead of crushing them, the hull principle of Nansen's ship Fram. In autumn they are towed into the forming pack ice and freeze in. They then ride the natural Transpolar Drift across the Arctic Ocean and reach Fram Strait in about one to two years, where tugs collect them near Svalbard. Every pod carries a satellite beacon, and a drift model updated with each year's ice-motion data picks the release points and dates that give the fastest, safest crossing.
value: Siberian bulk commodities reach the Atlantic with no fuel, icebreaker escort or Northern Sea Route fees; the main cost is a year or two of capital tied up in the cargo and the cheap hulls.

label: ctrl_7
name: Disposable pykrete flood barges
mech: Each winter, barge hulls 2–3 m thick are frozen in place at a mine's landing on a north-flowing river (Lena, Vilyuy, Yenisei, Kolyma). Water mixed with about 14% sawmill pulp is sprayed onto a mould layer by layer, and the −40 °C air does the freezing for free. The result, pykrete, is several times tougher than plain ice and melts slowly because a crust of insulating fibre forms on its surface. Ore concentrate or coal is loaded onto the deck during winter. The spring flood floats the hulls, and a few tugs guide convoys through the cold early meltwater to a transfer point in the river delta on the Northern Sea Route. There the cargo is lifted off and the hulls are left to melt. A hull costs only water, sawdust and pump fuel: no steel fleet sits idle, no barge makes an empty trip back upstream, and shallow tributaries are used only while the flood makes them deep.
value: Bulk cargo from deposits with no roads reaches Arctic shipping at almost no cost for the hulls.

label: ctrl_7
name: Spray-freeze mineral brine concentration
mech: Diamond pits on the Siberian Platform, such as Udachny, already pump out very salty brines and inject them back underground. These brines are rich in lithium, bromine, strontium and magnesium. In winter they are sprayed through snowmaking nozzles into −40 °C air. Almost pure water freezes out of the spray, and the salts stay behind in the liquid that has not frozen. That liquid drains from the bottom of the ice pile and is pumped to the next spray stage. A few stages reach concentrations that solar evaporation ponds take months to produce. The concentrate then goes to standard lithium and bromine recovery, and in spring the ice pile melts into nearly fresh water.
value: A waste stream that costs money to dispose of becomes a source of lithium and bromine, with winter cold doing the job of an evaporation pond and energy needed only for pumping.

label: ctrl_7
name: Autonomous kite-hauled sledge trains
mech: Strings of sledges on low-friction plastic runners carry concentrate, coal or equipment across frozen tundra, rivers and coastal sea ice. They are pulled by automated traction kites of 100–300 m² flying figure-eights, using the same control method already proven for kites that tow ships. Cold, dense air at −30 °C and the kites' figure-eight flight produce tens of kilonewtons of pull from the ordinary 6–8 m/s winter winds of Yamal and Taimyr, enough for tens of tonnes per kite. A small control unit plans routes from wind forecasts and satellite ice maps and can sail up to about 60° toward the wind. It anchors the train when the wind drops and follows GPS-marked snow corridors, so no graded road is needed. One remote operator supervises dozens of trains.
value: Deposits on the tundra and coasts of Yamal, Taimyr and Chukotka get freight with no fuel and no roads, at a fraction of what diesel trucks cost on winter roads.

label: ctrl_8
name: Under-ice river drift capsules
mech: Sealed plastic capsules of ore concentrate are lowered through an ice slot near the mine and carried north for months by the current still flowing under frozen Siberian rivers. Each trails a heavy guide chain: if it sinks, more chain rests on the riverbed and it gets lighter, so it holds height between bed and ice unpowered. A net hung from the ice downstream funnels capsules to a cut hole, acoustic tags track each one, and the port stockpiles them for summer shipping.
value: Turns the eight frozen months, when rivers carry nothing, into fuel-free freight far cheaper than winter-road trucking.

label: ctrl_8
name: Flood-launched disposable pykrete barges
mech: In winter, crews at the mine's riverbank spray water with about 14% sawdust into hollow barge moulds cut in shore ice, freezing thick hulls around sealed concentrate containers. After the spring ice run, the flood wave floats them free; one light tug pushes a convoy to the river mouth, where cargo moves to sea ships and hulls are broken up to melt. The sawdust's insulating skin slows melting enough for a two-to-four-week trip, and wall thickness is set from forecast water temperature and voyage length.
value: Lets mines on tributaries navigable only at flood peak ship bulk cargo with no steel fleet or return voyages.

label: ctrl_8
name: Arctic-air brine freeze pads
mech: Dilute brines, heap-leach liquors or mine water are sprayed through snow-making nozzles into -30 to -50°C air over lined pads, building cones of nearly salt-free ice while rejected brine drains to a sump. The sump liquor is re-sprayed in cycles until lithium, potassium or metal content reaches target, and in spring the salty first meltwater is collected separately. Spray rate tracks air temperature so freezing stays complete.
value: Gives Siberia a free equivalent of desert evaporation ponds, so brine minerals and leach metals are concentrated on site before shipping.

label: ctrl_6
name: Self-heating permafrost in-situ leaching
mech: Wells are drilled into a frozen sulfide orebody and warm acidic lixiviant is circulated, thawing only a bounded pocket while the surrounding ice-filled permafrost acts as a natural impermeable freeze wall that stops solution escaping. Sulfide oxidation is strongly exothermic, so once started the thawed zone heats itself; temperature and conductivity readings from monitoring wells set injection rates and oxidant dosing to grow the zone along the orebody and halt it at its edge. Metal is recovered on site as cathode or loaded resin, and at closure the zone refreezes, permanently locking residual solution in place.
value: Low-grade frozen copper, nickel and gold sulfide deposits become mineable without pits, mills, tailings dams or haul roads, shipping only finished metal.

label: ctrl_6
name: One-way insulated ice barges
mech: All winter, water is pumped in thin layers over a log-and-geotextile mat in a backwater beside the mine, freezing in -40°C air into a reinforced ice raft about three metres thick on which the mine stockpiles concentrate or coal. Before spring the raft is blanketed with sawdust, which preserves ice for months; at flood stage, after the ice run, the backwater connects to the river and a small tug steers the raft downstream to a railhead or trunk-river port. The cargo is unloaded and the raft left to melt, so there is no hull, shipyard or return voyage; each season's raft area is sized from measured ice thickness and planned tonnage.
value: Mines on tributaries too shallow for barges can ship over a thousand tonnes per raft for little more than the cost of winter pumping.

label: ctrl_6
name: Under-ice river capsule drift
mech: Concentrate is sealed in polyethylene sacks with an air pocket, then repeatedly wetted and frozen in -40°C air to build a smooth ice shell, giving spheres about 1.5 m across that carry roughly a tonne each and are just slightly buoyant. Through the winter they are slipped through a hole into a large river and roll along the underside of the ice cover with the current, in 0°C water that barely melts or thickens them, covering 30-50 km a day without fuel or vehicles. Downstream, an angled under-ice boom funnels them to a heated slot where a conveyor lifts them out; acoustic tags on a sample of spheres report transit times, and shell thickness is retuned whenever spheres stall or ground.
value: Frozen rivers become free conveyors for the seven months when barges are laid up, moving mine output to the nearest railhead.

label: EB:g2_evo2
name: Sun-thawed, wave-winnowed placer
anchor: heavy layer riding down a sun-driven thaw front
mech: The overburden is stripped from an ice-rich placer, and a small spillway holds a shallow pond of the ground's own meltwater on top. The dark water absorbs round-the-clock summer sun and thaws a few decimetres of gravel beneath it each season. Summer wind drives waves across the shallow pond, and they rework each freshly thawed layer the way surf works a beach: silt and light sand are lifted into suspension and leave over the spillway, while gold, heavy sands and coarse stones drop as a lag onto the still-frozen floor. Each year the spillway is lowered to keep the pond shallow, so the lag rides down with the thaw front to bedrock, and only that thin bottom layer is dug and washed.
value: Sun, wind and the deposit's own ice do the digging and most of the concentrating, so a placer is mined by moving a small fraction of its gravel, with no pumps, washing-plant fuel or reagents.

label: EB:g1_mech
name: Under-ice raw-ore drift
anchor: buoyant ore sacks carried under river ice by winter current
mech: Run-of-mine ore, neither crushed nor concentrated at the mine, is packed in tough 1 t sacks with a closed-cell foam collar that makes each sack slightly lighter than water. The sacks are pushed through a slot into a large river that keeps flowing under its ice all winter. They ride against the underside of the ice, and the current carries them roughly 10–40 km a day to a net under a slot at a downstream town that has power, where an ordinary mill separates the metal. Nobody chases sacks that snag: spring breakup frees them, and a boom at the same downstream site catches them in open water.
value: Because the river moves whole ore all winter with no fuel, a remote deposit needs no plant, power or reagents of its own, and separation happens where those already exist.

label: EB:g2_imm
name: Gold slugs in crude pipeline
anchor: metal riding an oil trunk line as tracked slugs
mech: At a pump station near a gold or platinum-metal deposit, a side stream of the line's own crude is dosed with a gold-selective extractant made only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (for example dibutyl carbitol, which does no harm in refining) and stirred with the deposit's chloride leach liquor. The precious metal moves into the oil and the stripped liquor goes back to the heap, so the reagents run in a closed loop and only metal leaves the site. The loaded crude rejoins the line as a density-tracked slug of about 2% of throughput, using the station's existing power and the pipeline's pumping. At the coastal terminal the slug is cut into its own tank and washed with hot oxalic acid, which drops the gold out as metal powder, and the crude is then exported as ordinary crude.
value: Precious metals from a roadless deposit reach a seaport with no trucks and no carrier to bring back, and the only inbound freight is a small top-up of leach reagent and extractant.

label: EB:g1_loop
name: Two-way ballast cassettes
anchor: ore cassettes replacing ballast water on LNG carriers
mech: Ice-class LNG carriers leave Arctic terminals below their weight limit and sail back empty, so both legs carry thousands of tonnes of seawater ballast. On the outbound leg, sealed cassettes of briquetted concentrate take the place of part of that ballast in double-bottom spaces, and they are swapped for seawater at the port where the LNG is unloaded. The empty return leg needs even more ballast, so the cassettes come back full of diesel, lime and process reagents for the mines. In summer, river barges on the Ob and Yenisei shuttle the cassettes between the deposits and the terminal.
value: A remote mine's concentrate goes out, and its fuel and reagents come in, on ships that sail the route anyway, so the supply line that makes on-site processing expensive costs almost nothing.

label: EB:g1_core2
name: Solar-etched yedoma barge canal
anchor: sun-thawed channel etched into ice-rich yedoma
mech: Along a surveyed line from a lowland deposit to a navigable river, the moss is stripped or darkened in a strip while insulating mats shield the edges, so meltwater pools in the strip and absorbs the 24-hour summer sun. Yedoma is often more than half ice, so each thawed layer collapses into mud that flows down the strip's slope and out to the river. This deepens the trench every summer until it reaches ice-poor ground at barge depth, and ground-temperature probes show where to darken again the next season. Once barges can reach the deposit, ore can leave unprocessed for a plant that already has power and reagents, so nothing has to be built on site.
value: Solar heat digs the access route, so a lowland deposit gets a barge channel for the cost of surface treatment instead of a road at millions of dollars per kilometre.

label: EB:g2_evo1
name: Submerged-stockpile winter sluicing
anchor: river under winter ice as free wash water
mech: In summer, placer gravel is dug and screened by gravity down to sand size. Before freeze-up the sand is heaped on a long riffle mat laid on the bed of a deep river reach that keeps flowing under its ice. Sitting under 0 °C water, the heap never freezes, and all winter the current wears it away grain by grain: light grains drift off, while gold and heavy minerals drop into the mat's riffles. In late winter the mat is pulled up through a slot in the ice and the concentrate is cleaned by hand.
value: Placer gold is washed through the whole winter with no pumps, heated plant or tailings pond, using the one thing in a Siberian winter that stays unfrozen.

label: EB:g1_genius
name: Fram-hulled pods on drift ice
anchor: ore pods riding the Transpolar Drift in sea ice
mech: Sealed, buoyant, satellite-tagged pods of concentrate have rounded, sledge-like hulls like Nansen's Fram, so when pressure ridges squeeze them they ride up onto the ice instead of being crushed. In winter the pods are set on young ice at the outer edge of the Laptev Sea fast ice near the Lena delta, where offshore winds push new ice north into the Transpolar Drift, which carries it to Fram Strait in 2–3 years. If a floe melts on the way, its pod simply floats on with the surface current and is frozen in again the next winter, and ships collect the pods in the open water of Fram Strait by their tag positions.
value: Bulk concentrate reaches European waters with no ship, fuel or icebreaker on the Arctic leg, and the only costs are the pods and the time.

label: EB:g1_core
name: Airlifted inflatable-weir barge staircase
anchor: airlifted inflatable weirs turning a stream into a barge staircase
mech: Folded rubber weirs are flown in and inflated in series on a small tributary between the deposit and a navigable river, and each pond fills with snowmelt and rain. Shallow-draft barges of concentrate wait in the top pond. Using simple level gauges, each gate release is timed and held just long enough to carry the barges over the next shallow stretch into the pond below, and empty barges are winched back up across the flat pools. The top pond's head also feeds the mine's washing water by gravity, and after the season the weirs are deflated and flown out, leaving no road or rail.
value: An ordinary summer stream becomes a temporary waterway, so bulk tonnage moves at water-freight cost without building a corridor.

label: EB:g2_imm
name: Leach-liquor freeze power plant
anchor: freezing under-ice water powers a cold-air engine
mech: Copper-bearing liquor from a summer heap leach is stored in a pond, where it stays liquid at 0–4 °C under the winter ice. It is pumped out and sprayed over coils, where it freezes into slush. The heat given off as it freezes boils propane, which drives a turbine and then condenses in finned radiators open to −35 to −50 °C air, so about 30 kg/s of liquor gives roughly 0.5–1 MW. Ice pushes out dissolved salts as it forms, so the brine that drains from the slush heaps is several times stronger than the feed and goes straight to an electrowinning cell run on the same power. Each kilogram of liquor frozen yields about 15–30 kJ of electricity, which is roughly what it takes to win the 1–2 g of copper it carries, and the cell turns the copper sulfate back into sulfuric acid, which returns to the heap with the ice meltwater in spring.
value: A remote copper deposit makes its own winter power and its own metal from its own leach liquor, with no diesel and almost no acid shipped in.

label: EB:g1_core
name: Snow-blanketed self-leaching copper outcrop
anchor: black film and snow fences ratchet ground heat
mech: On a gently sloping pyritic copper-sulfide outcrop, the thawed layer is ripped loose and left in place. Each spring it is covered with black geotextile that lets air and water through and soaks up the round-the-clock summer sun, and each autumn it is fenced so that drifting snow buries it under a thick insulating blanket. Once the ore is warm, bacteria oxidise its own pyrite, which makes sulfuric acid and heat; under the snow this keeps leaching going all winter, and the thaw front sinks deeper every year. In spring the snow the fences caught melts and flushes the dissolved copper down to the still-frozen floor, which acts as a natural liner and carries it downslope to a sump at the foot packed with scrap steel (old fuel drums litter northern sites), where the copper plates out as cement copper.
value: A shallow copper deposit leaches itself in place, using sun, snow and its own pyrite for heat, water and acid, and ships out only cement copper, with no plant, power line or reagent supply.

label: EB:g1_core2
name: Two-way ballistic supply line
anchor: ballistic freight with artillery-style fire correction
mech: Two fixed guns, one at the deposit and one at a railhead or river port more than 100 km away, fire steel-cased slugs of about 0.5 t at roughly 1.5 km/s into each other's sand-and-water catch basins. Radar measures where each slug lands, and the miss distance corrects the next shot, as in artillery adjusting fire. Casings fly out full of concentrate and come back full of diesel and reagents. Each inbound casing carries roughly two to three times the fuel the deposit's gun burns on an outbound shot, so the same loop powers the gun, the mill and the camp and needs no road, convoy or seasonal return route.
value: A stranded deposit is linked both ways all year, concentrate out and fuel and reagents in, by two fixed installations and no corridor at all.

label: EB:g2_evo2
name: Under-ice sphere freight
anchor: near-neutral spheres rolling under river ice
mech: Rigid spheres about 1 m across, with closed-cell foam shells, sealed holds and no gas, valves or electronics, are trimmed to about 0.5% positive buoyancy. They ride lightly against the smooth underside of a big Siberian river's winter ice and roll downstream with the current, and when they meet a hanging dam or a ridge the flow pushes them down and around it. Because these rivers flow north from the railway, spheres pushed through a slot at an upstream railhead carry diesel, brought to neutral buoyancy by dense reagents such as acid or lime in a second hold, down to a riverside mine. There they are emptied, refilled with concentrate, re-trimmed and pushed back under the ice to roll on to a boom at a downstream port, and the empties go back upriver by barge in summer.
value: Through the seven months when nothing else moves on the river, one under-ice current both supplies a riverside mine with fuel and reagents and carries its concentrate to port, with no vehicles, fuel or tending.

label: EB:g1_genius
name: Frozen-season tundra railway
anchor: winter-only track laid on frozen tundra
mech: Prefabricated track panels are laid straight onto frozen tundra compacted with snow, with no permanent embankment. Rivers are crossed on ice thickened by repeated flooding, tamping machines re-level the line each autumn to undo the summer heave, and trains run only in the 5–6 months when the ground is rigid. Because the line carries rail-scale tonnage at rail cost, it hauls raw ore, not concentrate, to a mill on the permanent rail network where grid power and reagents already exist, and the empty trains come back with fuel. The deposit therefore needs only a pit and a loading ramp, and nothing has to be separated in the cold.
value: Rail-scale bulk haulage reaches remote deposits for a fraction of the cost of an all-season Arctic railway, and lets them send raw ore to grid-powered mills instead of building a plant on permafrost.

label: EB:g2_evo1
name: Winter sublimation deflation pad
anchor: dry winter wind sublimes ore ice
mech: In deep winter, frozen placer gravel is ripped and spread in a thin layer on a pad at a windy tundra, coastal or ridge-top site. The dry −30 °C wind sublimes the pore ice from the top of the layer, freeing up to about a millimetre of sand a day, and because no liquid water ever forms, the freed grains lie loose and unbonded. The same wind then carries off the light quartz and feldspar grains, while gold, cassiterite, wolframite and other heavy grains (all but the finest) need a far stronger wind to move and stay behind with the gravel as a residue. A harrow turns the layer to expose fresh frozen sand, the residue is swept up and dry-screened to remove the gravel, and a snow fence downwind catches the blown waste sand.
value: Placer gold and heavy-mineral sands are concentrated in midwinter, when sluicing is impossible, with no water, fuel or reagent, using only the wind that dries them.

label: EB:g1_mech
name: Self-charging cold electrostatic separator
anchor: triboelectric sorting held by −40 °C dry air
mech: Dry crushed ore slides down a chute lined with a chosen material, so each mineral picks up its own sign of charge, and in −40 °C air, which holds almost no water vapour, that charge does not leak away. The grains fall between two plates into two metal-lined bins, and each bin is wired to the plate on the far side. The charge carried into the bins therefore keeps driving the plates to a higher voltage, as in a Kelvin water dropper, until a fixed spark gap caps the field at tens of kilovolts. The separator builds its own field from the ore's charge and gravity, with no power supply, water or reagent, and its only setting is the splitter between the bins, moved according to the grade measured in each bin.
value: Valuable minerals are separated from waste on site all winter with no water and no power for the separation itself, cutting the tonnage to be hauled by 5–20 times.

label: EB:g1_loop
name: Transpolar Drift cargo pods
anchor: Fram-hulled pods riding the Transpolar Drift
mech: Each autumn, sealed, buoyant pods with the hull shape of Nansen's Fram, so that ice pressure squeezes them upward instead of crushing them, are filled with coal or concentrate and set on newly formed Laptev Sea ice. The Transpolar Drift carries them to the ice edge in Fram Strait in about two years, where an ordinary ship collects them by beacon; if their floe melts early, they float on with the same currents. Launch sites are chosen from satellite ice-motion maps traced backward from Fram Strait, keeping only starting points whose paths reliably lead out rather than into the Beaufort Gyre, and the choice is updated each season from the pods' beacon logs.
value: Bulk cargo moves from the Laptev coast to the North Atlantic with no engines, icebreakers or port, trading about two years in transit for almost no freight cost.

label: EB:g1_core2
name: Sky-cooled lithium brine freeze-out
anchor: sky-radiating film running below air temperature
mech: Deep Yakutian mines pump out strong calcium-chloride drainage brine that they then have to get rid of. Here it is frozen in shallow batch trays covered with polymer radiative-cooling film under a thin infrared-clear windshield, so it sheds heat straight to space through the 8–13 µm atmospheric window and runs about 10 K colder than the winter air. On nights below about −40 °C this takes the brine past the calcium chloride–ice eutectic (about −50 °C). Ice and calcium chloride hexahydrate freeze out together as a crust, while lithium chloride, which stays liquid down to roughly −75 °C, gathers in a shrinking leftover liquid that drains by gravity into a covered sump. Every degree the film reaches below the eutectic leaves that liquid smaller and richer, so the sky's cold sets the lithium grade, not fuel or reagents.
value: Mine waste brine becomes a lithium concentrate using only the winter sky, with no fuel, reagents or evaporation ponds.

label: EB:g2_imm
name: Nickel carbonyl through gas pipelines
anchor: nickel carbonyl riding in pipeline gas
mech: Beside a gas trunk line, a small side stream of the line's own gas is partly burned to hot carbon monoxide and hydrogen. This gas first reduces roasted nickel ore to metal; then, cooled to about 50 °C at a few bar, it carries the nickel off as nickel tetracarbonyl vapour. Iron, copper and rock barely react under these mild conditions, so this one step does the whole separation with a reagent made only from the line's gas. The vapour is metered into the line at about 0.1 mol%, which keeps it below its condensation pressure even in the coldest permafrost-chilled sections, and a little extra carbon monoxide stops it breaking down in warm compressor stations. At the receiving terminal, before any customer, beds at about 200 °C split it into pure nickel pellets and carbon monoxide, which is burned or sent back.
value: A line carrying about 38 billion m³ of gas a year could also deliver roughly 100,000 t of refined nickel a year from a remote deposit, with no new transport route and no reagent brought in.

label: EB:g1_genius
name: Cold-shatter dry placer winnowing
anchor: deep-frozen ice as a brittle, light mineral
mech: Frozen placer gravel is dug in deep winter and fed, still below −30 °C, through a light impact breaker. The ice cement is by far the weakest phase, so it shatters into chips and dust while pebbles and gold grains stay whole, and almost all the crushing energy goes into the ice. A screen drops the coarse pebbles, and a rising air stream blows the ice fragments and silt off the rest, because ice is about 20 times lighter than gold and 3 times lighter than quartz. That leaves a small sand-and-gold residue for a dry air table. At −30 °C the air is so dry that nothing clumps, no water or reagent is used, and the ice-and-gravel tailings are stacked frozen.
value: Placer gold can be recovered all winter straight from frozen ground with little power and no thawing, water, ponds or reagents.

label: EB:g1_core
name: Ore-floored solar leach pond
anchor: summer-heated brine pond discharged to −40 °C air
mech: An insulated, lined salt-gradient pond is floored with about a metre of crushed chalcocite-rich copper ore. The dark ore absorbs sunlight like a solar pond's black bottom and sits all year in the 60–80 °C chloride bottom brine, which also serves as the leach liquor. In winter the hot brine runs an organic Rankine cycle that dumps its heat into −40 °C air at roughly twice the efficiency of temperate solar ponds. The electricity drives a divided cell: brine drawn from under the ore bed flows through it, cuprous copper plates out as powder at the cathode, and the anode turns cuprous into cupric chloride, which goes back to attack the ore. Overall the chalcocite simply splits into copper metal and sulfur, so no acid, oxygen or other reagent is used up, and the energy cost is well under a kilowatt-hour per kilogram of copper.
value: A remote chalcocite copper deposit can make copper metal all winter from local salt and summer sun, with no fuel, acid, oxygen plant or power line.

label: EB:g1_loop
name: Under-ice drifting ore pods
anchor: buoyant pods riding under river ice
mech: In winter, slightly buoyant torpedo-shaped pods are pushed through a slot cut in the ice of a big river's main channel. They float up against the smooth underside of the ice and ride the current, out of reach of wind and waves, to a boom and recovery slot at a downstream port; where a slush dam blocks the flow, a relay slot lifts them past it. Because the haul burns no fuel, the pods can carry crushed high-grade ore instead of concentrate, so the mine needs no flotation plant, power or reagents of its own. Separation happens at the port or smelter, where those already exist, and the collapsible pods go back upstream by summer barge.
value: Remote deposits can send ore to Arctic ports all through the frozen months without fuel, vessels or a processing plant at the mine.

label: EB:g1_mech
name: Ice-dam sluice and crest barging
anchor: winter ice dam releasing a timed snowmelt crest
mech: In winter, water sprayed across a small creek builds an ice dam, a peat cover keeps it from melting, and snowmelt fills the basin behind it. In midsummer the gate first lets a steady flow down a riffled chute beside the dam, into which thawed tin or tungsten placer gravel is fed. The heavy ore minerals settle in the riffles and the light gravel is swept into a dug pit, so the stored water and its head do the whole separation with no pumps, fuel or reagents. Then the gate opens fully, and the crest floats flat-bottomed barges of concentrate down to a river deep enough for ships.
value: A roadless placer gets free process water, a free gravity concentrator and a free summer freight route from one winter's snow.

label: EB:g2_evo1
name: Snow-sculpted under-ice ore groove
anchor: snow-cleared strips sculpting an under-ice groove
mech: In early winter, two parallel strips along a frozen river's fast main channel are kept clear of snow, while the snow between and beside them is left as insulation. The ice grows faster under the bare strips and forms two downward keels with a smooth groove between them on the ice's underside. Slightly buoyant pods of crushed high-grade ore, put in through a slot, float up into the groove and ride the current between the keels, so they cannot stray into slow water near the banks; the strips are simply cleared again after each snowfall. Because the conveyor builds itself and burns no fuel, ore can ship without being concentrated, leaving separation to the port or smelter, which already has power and reagents.
value: Any large frozen river becomes a self-built, fuel-free winter conveyor that takes ore away from a remote mine with no road, vessel or processing plant.

label: EC:EB:g1_loop
name: Whole-Ore Ballast Swap
anchor: ore cassettes swapped for LNG-carrier ballast
mech: Ice-class LNG carriers fill up by volume long before they reach their weight limit, so both legs from Arctic terminals carry thousands of tonnes of seawater ballast. That is far more free tonnage than any mine's concentrate. Sealed cassettes of crushed but unconcentrated ore take the place of that ballast in the double-bottom spaces and are swapped for seawater at the port where the LNG is unloaded. An ordinary mill there, with grid power and cheap reagents, separates the metal. On the empty return leg the cassettes come back full of diesel, and summer river barges on the Ob and Yenisei shuttle them between the deposits and the terminal, so the mine itself runs only drills, loaders and a crusher.
value: A remote Arctic mine can do without its concentrator, power plant and reagent supply altogether, because the hard step of separating metal moves to a warm, powered port on freight that is already paid for.

label: EC:EB:g1_mech
name: Ice-Shell Under-Ice Ore Drift
anchor: buoyant ore packages drifting under river ice
mech: Run-of-mine ore goes into 1 t sacks, each with a thin plastic air bladder, and is frozen into a shell of river water in a simple mould. The trapped air plus the ice make each package slightly lighter than water, so the float itself comes free from the winter and nothing has to be shipped back upstream. The packages sit in a slot pool until they warm to 0 °C and are then pushed under the ice of a large river that flows all winter. In 0 °C water the shell cannot melt, and the current carries the packages 10–40 km a day to a net under a slot at a downstream town with power, where an ordinary mill separates the metal and the shells melt away. Packages that snag are freed at breakup and caught by a boom at the same site, and the only consumable is one liner per tonne.
value: Moving whole ore costs almost nothing per tonne and nothing returns upstream, so even ordinary-grade deposits upriver of a powered town need no plant, power, reagents or return freight of their own.

label: EC:EB:g1_core
name: Pulse-Sorting Weir Staircase
anchor: inflatable weir staircase releasing timed flood pulses
mech: Folded rubber weirs are flown in and inflated in series on a small tributary below a deposit, where they store snowmelt and rain in a chain of ponds. Frost-broken ore is spread in a riffled side lane of the stretch below each weir. Each timed gate release sends a measured flood pulse over the ore that sweeps clay, silt and light rock into the next pond, where they settle as tailings, while gold, cassiterite, diamonds or other heavy minerals stay in the riffles to be scooped out. The same pulses carry shallow-draft barges of this concentrate over each shallow stretch to the navigable river, and after the season the weirs are deflated and flown out, leaving no road, plant or tailings dam.
value: A roadless placer or heavy-mineral deposit gets its washing plant, tailings ponds and haul route from one seasonal staircase of water, with no pumps, fuel or reagents.

label: EC:EB:g2_evo1
name: Snow-Sculpted Under-Ice Sluice
anchor: under-ice current washing a sand heap over a riffle mat
mech: Before freeze-up, placer sand screened in summer is laid as a long windrow beside a riffle mat on the bed of a river reach that keeps flowing all winter. Through the winter, snow is scraped off a band of ice across the reach above the mat and piled on the ice upstream and downstream of it. Bare ice grows much faster than snow-covered ice, so the band grows a keel that squeezes the whole river's flow beneath it and speeds up the current over the windrow, faster each month as the keel deepens. The faster current strips the windrow grain by grain: light grains leave downstream, gold and heavy minerals drop into the riffles, and in late winter the mat is lifted through a slot and the concentrate is cleaned by hand.
value: A placer mine can wash a full season's sand during winter at several times the natural under-ice rate, with frost building the sluice and the river powering it, so the short summer is spent only digging and no washing fuel, pumps or heated plant are needed.

label: EC:EB:g1_core2
name: Lake-Breach Thermo-Erosion Canal
anchor: darkened strip steering thermokarst into a channel
mech: Along a surveyed line from a lowland deposit to a navigable river, the moss is stripped or darkened in a strip with insulating mats along its edges, so the ground beneath thaws first and becomes the weakest path. A sun-warmed thaw lake or a dammed creek at the deposit end is then breached into the strip. Its 10–15 °C water runs down the line, melts the ice-rich yedoma at metres per day by thermo-erosion and carries the collapsing silt to the river. This is the same process that cuts gullies metres deep in days when such lakes drain naturally. Ground-temperature probes show where to darken further before the next lake is released, and once barges can reach the deposit the ore leaves unprocessed for a plant that already has power and reagents.
value: Summer heat stored in lakes digs a barge channel in one or two seasons instead of decades, so a roadless lowland deposit is opened to water freight without building a road.

label: EC:EB:g2_evo2
name: Self-Sorting Wave-and-Ice Pond
anchor: wind-wave pond winnowing a placer as it thaws
mech: Over a stripped, ice-rich placer, a spillway holds a shallow pond of the ground's own meltwater. The pond absorbs the round-the-clock summer sun and thaws the gravel beneath it, wind waves lift silt and sand over the spillway, and their pressure pulses jig gold and heavy sand down through the stones onto the frozen floor. Each autumn the pond is set just shallower than the winter ice will grow, so the ice freezes onto the tops of the stones. In spring the spillway is closed, snowmelt lifts the bottom-fast ice, and the wind pushes the floes and their stones onto a dump shore, the way lake ice builds boulder ramparts. The spillway is lowered each year so the thin heavy layer rides down with the thaw front to bedrock, where only that layer is dug and washed.
value: Even in the cobbly gravels typical of Siberian placers, sun, wind and winter ice remove the silt, sand and stones in place, so only a few percent of the deposit is ever dug and washed, with no pumps, washing-plant fuel or reagents.

label: EC:EB:g2_imm
name: Cold-Brine Leach, Crude-Carried Gold
anchor: crude-oil slug carrying extracted gold to the coast
mech: At a crude-oil pump station near a gold or platinum-metal deposit, ore is heap-leached all year with a strong calcium chloride brine that stays liquid far below −30 °C. The chlorine and acid the leach needs are made on site by electrolysing a bleed of the same brine with the station's existing power, so only top-up salt is shipped in. A side stream of the line's own crude, dosed with a gold extractant made only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen such as dibutyl carbitol, is stirred once through the metal-loaded brine and rejoins the line as a density-tracked slug. As a result the site needs no carbon columns, elution, electrowinning, smelter or gold room. At the coastal terminal the slug is cut into its own tank and washed with hot oxalic acid, which drops the gold out as metal powder, and the crude is exported as ordinary crude.
value: A deposit beside a crude pipeline can leach and recover precious metal right through the Siberian winter with only a heap, a mixer and an electrolysis cell on site and only salt brought in.

label: EC:EB:g1_genius
name: River-to-Pole Drift Pods
anchor: Fram-hulled pods riding the Transpolar Drift
mech: Sealed, buoyant, satellite-tagged pods with rounded, sledge-like hulls like Nansen's Fram ride up instead of being crushed when ice squeezes them. They are filled at the deposit itself and launched into a north-flowing river such as the Lena, Yana or Indigirka, whose summer current carries them to the delta with no barge or fuel. A boom at the delta gathers the pods. In early winter they are hauled over the fast ice and set on young ice at its outer edge, where offshore winds push the new ice into the Transpolar Drift, which carries it to Fram Strait in 2–3 years. A pod freed by melt floats on and is frozen in again the next winter. Because no leg of the route costs anything per tonne-kilometre, the pods can carry screened run-of-mine ore instead of concentrate, and ships collect them by tag position and take them to a European plant that has the power and reagents to separate the metal.
value: A roadless deposit on any Arctic-draining river can send its ore to a powered plant with no road, barge, icebreaker, fuel or on-site concentrator.
